margined.summary: Salinas to Fuenmayor, London 21 Aug 1676: Charles II tells Salinas that an invasion of France would harm the peace and that the Maastricht and Philippsburg sieges will end the campaign; the King is in a bad humour over German successes; on the passports he favours the Münster precedent against the princes' new claims (Lorraine); no treaty talk until the campaign ends.
margined.en:
⟨... of the much that can be done.⟩ Although, in a long conference I had with the King, he told me that [the] entry
into France would rather harm the peace than advance it, so that, though we must [...] believe the opposite, we
should suppose it for the best; and when I told him that the other siege could not be avoided, he said that with these
two fortresses being taken the campaign would end; whose malign counsels I fear may influence the Nephew.

The King is in a bad humour these days, and it is believed that the good fortune of the Germans has a part in it; for,
though there is no other talk than that of these sieges, counting down to the last musketeer lost in it, he has kept
quiet the favourable news, which Courtin has not done with more gallantry.

On the business of the protest there has been no further talk;

unmargined.summary: Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen 19 Mar 1678: after the loss of Ghent Flanders is near despair; England stays irresolute; he hopes the allies drop their quarrels to defend the Low Countries and the North; Königsmarck's incursion should press the Brunswick princes; nothing worth reporting from the congress.
unmargined.en:
⟨... with which the favours Your Lordship does me continue.⟩ [...] I have read with particular pleasure Your
Lordship's reflections and what [...] moving towards the steps, which are very much in keeping with Your Lordship's
prudence, zeal and [?energy]. And would to God our misfortunes were not so overwhelming [...] we found ourselves in a
position to [...]; but as they are of the bad kind Your Lordship [?will have] understood, we must resign ourselves to
the will of God and ascribe to His just judgements that Flanders should run [...] to the last despair, which, [?I
assure] Your Lordship, leaves us all [?so] astonished and taken by surprise that even the pleasure of discussing with
the [...] fails us, [...] the grief and the thought of our misfortune.
